newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Cargo flow rises along Africa's Beira corridor.
newsitem.headline: Cargo flow rises along Africa's Beira corridor.

text.p: Cargo movements along the Zimbabwe-Beira road/rail corridor rose by 11 percent in 1996, and a top industry official said on Tuesday a bumper harvest in 1997 may further raise exports and business for one of southern Africa's key trade routes.

David Zausmer, managing director of the Beira Corridor Group (BCG), also told Reuters that sponsorship of business development along the 500-km (300 mile) corridor would start to take shape from mid-year.
"The bottom line is -- the prospects are looking very good. Cargo flow is increasing, and facilities in the corridor, and at the port, are being continually improved," he said.
Beira port on the Indian Ocean handles cargo ranging from cotton to coal to and from landlocked Botswana, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, and also for Mozambique.

The corridor, which also includes an oil pipeline to Zimbabwe, fell victim to Mozambique's civil war but was rehabilitated in the late 1980s to lessen southern Africa's dependence on trade routes through then-apartheid South Africa.
Business has risen steadily over the years, Zausmer said.
Total export traffic through the Beira corridor rose by two percent in 1996 while import container traffic increased by 29 percent during the year.
Zausmer said he hoped the Beira Development Corridor programme would see progress from mid-year when regional governments were expected to have processed legal papers setting up the project.
"For us it's a long-term project...and it should be able to generate itself once people stop looking at things in isolation," the BCG chief said.
He said there was potential to develop sugar estates in eastern Mozambique and huge cotton farms in southern Malawi if Malawi's Sena rail corridor into Mozambique was rehabilitated.
"We have to link our transport development with general business developments," Zausmer said.
